# OECD Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026

## Chapter 1. Digital priorities, policies and governance 

### Abstract 

Using newly collected data from OECD Member countries and partner economies and the OECD Going Digital Integrated Policy Framework 2026 as a guide, this chapter examines trends in digital policy priorities. It finds that while digital government has consistently been the top digital policy priority over the past decade, cybersecurity and technology development became more important in 2025. It also analyses national digital strategies in the countries in which they exist and the governance approaches in place to design, implement and monitor them. The data show that responsibility for developing and co-ordinating national digital strategies is increasingly led by dedicated digital ministries rather than at the centre of government. Finally, the chapter explores the broader digital policy landscape. It shows that technology-neutral policymaking is giving way to technology-specific digital policies, and that most digital policies today aim at increasing effective use, unleashing digital innovation, and societal issues.

### Key findings 

 Digital government remains the top digital policy priority, with growing focus on cybersecurity and technology development

- Connectivity, skills, cybersecurity and technology development were regularly ranked in the top five of countries’ digital policy priorities from 2016 to 2025. As of 2025, cybersecurity emerged as the second highest digital priority among the OECD Member countries and partner economies surveyed.
- Over the past decade, digital government has consistently ranked as the top digital policy priority in the OECD Member countries and partner economies for which comparable data exist.

 Responsibility for developing and co-ordinating national digital strategies is increasingly led by dedicated digital ministries rather than at the centre of government

- The share of OECD Member countries and partner economies that assign primary responsibility for developing their national digital strategy to dedicated digital ministries reached 60% in 2025, up from just 24% in 2016. Of these countries, 68% also assign co-ordination tasks to a dedicated digital ministry or body.
- In parallel, the share of national digital strategies developed at above ministerial level (such as the Prime Minister’s Office, Presidency or Chancellery) declined from 42% in 2023 to 26% in 2025.

 The digital policy landscape is characterised by initiatives that aim to increase effective use and unleash digital innovation, as well as societal issues

- Among the almost 1 500 policy initiatives collected across 42 OECD Member countries and partner economies in 2025, about 40% focus on effective use of digital technologies, 30% on digital innovation and 28% on societal issues.
- Skills is the most prominent policy domain in the digital policy landscape, with initiatives concentrated on improving information and communication technology skills across demographic groups.

 Technology-neutral policymaking is giving way to technology-specific digital policies

- “Artificial intelligence” is the most oft-cited term in digital policies over 2023-2025, reflecting the ubiquity of the technology and its importance to policymakers.
- As of 2023, quantum technologies, semiconductors and satellites have become more prominent in digital policy initiatives. This is exemplified by the emergence of dedicated semiconductor strategies and an increasing focus on quantum computing, communications and sensing, and low earth orbit satellites.

### Introduction 

Digital technologies and data shape how individuals, businesses and governments live, work, communicate and access services. As digital transformation accelerates across sectors, addressing digital policy issues across silos has become essential to ensure coherent and effective policy responses that maximise the opportunities of digital technologies while managing risks. In this context, greater understanding of the digital policy landscape across countries provides critical insights for effective policymaking.

The OECD Going Digital Integrated Policy Framework 2026 (hereafter “the Framework”) (OECD, 2026 [1]), provides a flexible, whole-of-government approach to developing digital policies (Annex 1.A). Using the Framework as a guide, this chapter is informed by responses to the OECD Digital Economy and Society Outlook (DESO) 2026 data collection. It examines trends in digital policy priorities across countries; analyses national digital strategies in the countries for which they exist and the governance approaches in place to design, implement and monitor them; and explores the broader digital policy landscape across countries.

### Box 1.1. Surveying digital policies yields valuable insights, but qualitative surveys come with caveats 

 Copy link to Box 1.1. Surveying digital policies yields valuable insights, but qualitative surveys come with caveats 

The analysis in this chapter is based on the three parts of the DESO 2026 data collection: national digital strategies 1 (see Annex 1.B) and their governance arrangements; digital policy priorities (Annex 1.C); and digital policy initiatives (excluding national digital strategies). The latter part includes information on the following special topics: children in digital environments; media and digital literacy initiatives; and policies to support older adults in the digital age.

References to “countries” in this chapter reflect the OECD Member countries and partner economies that responded to data collections for the OECD Digital Economy Outlook (DEO) 2017, 2020 and 2024. New data from the DESO 2026 data collection appear in three parts. Part 1 reflects data from 42 countries on national digital strategies and governance arrangements, 7 of which reported having no strategy. Part 2 comprises data from the same countries on their digital policy priorities, 16 of which provided no priority ranking and 4 of which provided incomplete data. Part 3 comprises information from 42 countries on major digital policies, including the special focus topics.

The DESO 2026 data collection was administered to OECD Member countries and partner economies that are actively involved in the work of the OECD Digital Policy Committee, the OECD’s lead digital policy and measurement body. Not every country responded to each part of the data collection; a full list of countries covered for each part can be found in the Annex 1.D.

Policy survey data provide comparable insights on countries’ policymaking approaches and enable the categorisation and quantification of information, but the data come with important caveats. For example, the data emphasise the number of policy initiatives rather than their actual impact, offering a view of what exists rather than how well it works. In addition, the responses are typically shaped by the perspectives of the policymakers completing the surveys, who may interpret questions differently. Since there is no agreed definition of “digital policy” across and within countries, it is unlikely that such surveys capture all relevant initiatives.

Note: The country coverage for each part of the 2017, 2020, 2024 and 2026 data collections can be found in Annex 1.D.

1. The national digital strategy list provided in Annex 1.B is based on the DESO 2026 data collection and desk research.

### Digital government remains the top digital policy priority, with growing focus on cybersecurity and technology development 

 Copy link to Digital government remains the top digital policy priority, with growing focus on cybersecurity and technology development 

Since 2016, digital government has been identified as governments’ top digital policy priority (Table 1.1). This reflects the recognition that digital technologies are essential to improving public service delivery, strengthening trust in government and enhancing policy effectiveness. Governments are increasingly investing in digital technologies and data to make services more user-centric, data-driven and accessible, while also improving administrative efficiency and resilience.

In 2025, cybersecurity emerged as the second most important digital policy priority across countries for the first time in the ten years these data have been collected. This move reflects a recognition by governments of the need to protect critical infrastructure, public services, economic activity and citizens from an increasingly complex and evolving threat landscape. The rise of cybersecurity in digital policy agendas suggests that policymakers are increasingly concerned about the risks associated with cyber incidents, including financial and reputational damage, and potential disruptions to critical activities.

Technology development and diffusion also moved to its highest position in 2025 – tied for third position with connectivity and skills. 1 Policymakers increasingly recognise that targeted investment in digital research and development, alongside the availability of key enabling resources such as data, capital, digital infrastructure and digital skills, is critical. Together, they strengthen national technological capabilities and accelerate adoption of digital technologies by individuals and businesses to support productivity, competitiveness, innovation and economic growth.

The 2025 ranking of digital policy priorities suggests that the top priorities across countries are becoming more diverse. A relatively smaller number of top priorities were identified in 2016, 2019 and 2023, but three priorities in 2025 were tied for third place (connectivity, skills, and technology development and diffusion). At the same time, some top priorities have been relatively constant over the last decade – digital government, connectivity and skills have remained at the top of the priority list. This indicates strong continuity with previous years despite the fast-changing digital technology landscape.

Four of the five countries from the Latin American and the Caribbean (LAC) region that responded to the DESO 2026 data collection ranked “digital inclusion” as one of their top three digital policy priorities. The strong emphasis on this priority suggests that enhancing participation in digital economies and societies across a range of characteristics, such as age, education level, firm size, geography, income level or sex, is considered a foundational step for advancing the region’s digital development. Moreover, these five LAC countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Costa Rica) all include references to “digital inclusion” in their national digital strategies, either underpinned by the need to increase access to connectivity services and infrastructure or to promote skills development among the population.
